title: Rural Ontario residents slam proposed land-seizure powers for Alto high-speed rail project
summary: Some rural residents are speaking out against sweeping powers the federal government is proposing to help clear the way for Canada's first high-speed rail project, which they say leave their concerns…

blocks.text: Ottawa

Some rural residents are speaking out against sweeping powers the federal government is proposing to help clear the way for Canada's first high-speed rail project, which they say leave their concerns in the dust.
The federal government is proposing to scrap standard expropriation rules
· CBC News
· Posted: Nov 25, 2026 8:00 AM EST | Last Updated: 3 hours ago
The feds are proposing rule changes for Alto. What could it mean for landowners?

The Alto project linking Toronto and Quebec City was announced late last year with planned stops in Trois-Rivières, Laval, Montreal, Ottawa and Peterborough. Its CEO said this summer that it would likely add a stop in Kingston for some of its electric trains.
The government's latest cost estimate is $60 billion to $90 billion, and the federal budget watchdog said recently that could balloon by another $15 billion to $25 billion.

If passed in the bill for the latest federal budget, the government could expropriate land without public hearings, transfer ownership directly to a private consortium and send unresolved crossing disputes for split farms and municipal roads to private arbitration.

items: Sweeping new land-seizure powers proposed for high-speed rail project

blocks.text: Some residents around the possible route fear the changes would sacrifice their homes and properties while leaving them with few ways to fight back.
"It's very, very concerning," said Mike MacGillivray, whose family has been working at Kirkview Farms in North Glengarry, Ont., for eight generations.
MacGillivray described the proposed exemptions as "powers of a king," and said he now worries for the farm's future since it is within the study corridor.

Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon defended the move, calling the project "nation-building." He added that the "land acquisition regime is going to provide a number of layers of flexibility," including letting people stay on their land even after it is acquired.
"It will be the spinal cord of mobility in the corridor.… It will allow people to live, play, study in one place and do activities in other cities," he said in Ottawa Tuesday.
"This is a 60-meter corridor. This is not proposing to take large swaths of land. This is going to be a bespoke regime."
High-speed rail expropriation will go through 'bespoke' process, MacKinnon says
When asked if the minister's words brought him any comfort about the project, MacGillivray said they did not.
"It isn't [a] nation building project. It's anything but," he said.

"The concern is that the assurances that are being given are just words and they actually speak volumes to the fact that they don't understand the implications of a project like this on the farming community, on rural communities and the impact it has on food security."

blocks.text: Under one proposed change, the government could have right of first refusal, for eight years, to make an offer on a property.

Those in the identified corridor also would not be able to develop their property for up to four years. These restrictions are even before the government decides whether it wants to expropriate the land at all.
"The early reaction … has been quite outraged," said lawyer Erin Durant, who lives in Alto's study corridor.
She said the bill should be taken out of the Budget Implementation Act so it can be voted on separately.
Lawyer Erin Durant lives within Alto's study corridor and says she has heard from many people worried about the impact high-speed rail could have on their property. (Dan Taekema)
In a statement to CBC, Alto spokesperson Marlee Socket emphasized the government is responsible for the bill.
However, she said building high-speed rail requires a new framework for acquiring land.
"The proposed measures would help us move forward responsibly toward the start of construction in 2029–2030," Socket's email read.
"A more streamlined process does not mean reducing protections for affected property owners or project oversight."
Alto will prioritize negotiated agreements, she wrote, and compensation will be based on the circumstances of each property or farm, including its value and impacts over time.
